canvas-05.description: Sheet 1 of Volume One covers a block of South Camden rowhouse streets between Washington Street at the top and Beckett Street at the bottom, with South 3rd Street running down the right-centre of the sheet and South 2nd Street near the left edge; South 4th Street is cut by the right margin. The cross streets are Washington, Berkley, Clinton, Royden and Beckett, with the narrow alleys Senate and Evans between them. Nearly every block is a regular grid of two and three storey brick dwellings, marked D on the sheet, built in long terraces with narrow yards behind and small yellow frame outbuildings at the rear. A few lots hold stores and a club room. The lower left corner, beyond South 2nd Street, is a different kind of ground: it is the factory frontage on Spring Street, with the Strandwitz & Scott Inc. sheet metal works and the Camden Copper Works (forge shop, sheet copper working, pattern store), both marked as having no watchman. Peach Street reaches the bottom left. The left part of the sheet above that, west of South 2nd Street, is blank paper belonging to the neighbouring sheet 50. The bottom margin carries the printed notice See Camden Volume Three, and the blocks beyond Beckett Street are left empty for that volume. Water mains of 4, 6, 8 and 16 inches are drawn in every street with their sizes, and street widths of 60 and 66 feet are marked. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the street grid turned about 7 degrees from the page. Adjoining sheets are 9 above, 2 to the right and 50 and 51 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 1; the previous-edition number under it is cut off at the left edge of the scan.
The street grid on the sheet is turned about 7 degrees from the page; the fitted scale is about 8.07 pixels per foot, as expected for 50 feet to an inch.
Senate and Evans survive only as service alleys in OpenStreetMap and were not used as control; South 2nd Street survives only near Clinton Street.
The South 4th Street junctions lie at or beyond the right edge of the scan; their positions rest on the drawn edge plus half the street width.
printed sheet 1, 50 ft: Washington to Beckett, S 2nd to S 4th

canvas-07.description: Sheet 2 covers the South Camden blocks between Washington Street at the top and Line Street at the bottom, from South 4th Street on the left to South 5th Street on the right, with West Street dividing the sheet into two halves. The cross streets are Washington, Berkley, Clinton, Royden and Beckett, with Senate and Evans as alleys, Riley and Avon as short side streets and Henry Street running down the right half. The left half is the better built: long terraces of two and three storey dwellings on Clinton, Evans and Royden, and two public schools, the E. A. Stevens Public School at Washington and Riley Streets and the Central Public School on Senate Street. The Keystone Telephone Co. exchange stands on Berkley Street, and Peech Sons & Phillips yarn winding and mercerizing works occupies much of the block between Senate and Clinton Streets. On the right half of the sheet the blocks east of West Street are drawn with a mixture of brick dwellings and frame buildings, and include a metal plating and welding shop, a wood working plant and a private garage. West Street is drawn with a jog, so that Washington Street meets it in two places about 90 feet apart. The right margin shows empty outlines of blocks belonging to the neighbouring sheets, and the bottom margin carries the notice See Camden Volume Three. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with a north arrow turned about 7 degrees from the page; the sheet adjoins 1 on the left, 3 on the right and 10 above.
notes: Printed sheet number 2; previous edition sheet 6 of volume 2.
Senate, Evans, Riley, Avon and Henry survive only as service alleys or not at all in OpenStreetMap and were not used as control.
Washington Street jogs at West Street in the modern street network as well as on the sheet; both junctions were used.
printed sheet 2 (6 vol 2), 50 ft: Washington to Line, S 4th to S 5th, West Street jog

canvas-09.description: Sheet 3 covers the blocks around Broadway in South Camden, from Washington Street at the top to Line Street at the bottom, between South 5th Street on the left and South 6th Street on the right. Broadway runs down the middle of the sheet, with William Street to its west and Saint John Street to its east. The largest works is the Freihofer Baking Company, Camden plant, which fills the upper left blocks with its bake houses, ovens, loading platforms, wagon shed and private garages (capacity 20 and 50 cars). Churches face Broadway: the Broadway M.E. Church between Berkley and Clinton Streets and St. John's Episcopal Church with its rectory and guild house between Clinton and Royden Streets. Opposite stand the Broadway Public School, an undertaker's fireproof building dated 1920, and the Camden Free Public Library near Line Street. The rest of the sheet is rowhouse blocks, with two and three storey brick dwellings along the cross streets, shops on Broadway, a boarding house called The Carteret at the top right, and a gold leaf manufactory near South 5th Street. Water mains and street widths of 40, 60 and 66 feet are marked. The bottom margin shows blank block outlines under the notice See Camden Volume Three. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and its north arrow is turned slightly to the left of the page; it adjoins sheet 2 on the left, 4 on the right and 11 above.
notes: Printed sheet number 3; the previous-edition number under it is cut off at the left edge of the scan.
William and Saint John Street survive only as service streets in OpenStreetMap (Williams Street, Saint John Street) and were not used as control.
The Broadway / Line Street junction in OpenStreetMap lies about 7 m from the drawn junction and was rejected by the fit.
This sheet fits at a rotation of about -2.4 degrees, against about -7 degrees for sheets 1, 2, 9 and 10 to its west: the sheets are scanned or drawn at slightly different angles.
printed sheet 3, 50 ft: Washington to Line, Broadway

canvas-11.description: Sheet 4 covers the district on both sides of South 7th Street in South Camden, where the Pennsylvania Railroad's West Jersey and Seashore electric line runs down the street in a strip about 125 feet wide. West of it, between Washington Street at the top and Line Street at the bottom, are regular rowhouse blocks along Chambers Avenue, Roberts Street and Felton Street, with Berkley, Clinton and Royden Streets crossing them. Most of the dwellings are two storey brick rows, with a few frame houses and a small group of buildings at Roberts Court. The one large building is the Werner Storage Ware Ho. Corpn. warehouse, between Clinton and Royden Streets. East of South 7th Street the grid is cut by two diagonal avenues. Washington Street and Trenton Avenue run to the north-east, and Newton Avenue runs along the bottom right, so that the blocks between them are wedges and triangles filled with dwellings. Within them lie New Street, Berkley Street, Edmunds Street and Blaine Street, and Line Street appears again at the bottom right. Seward Street and South 8th Street are drawn at the right edge. Street widths of 20 to 60 feet are marked, and the PRR right of way carries heights of 114 and 125 feet. The bottom and right margins show blank outlines under the notice See Camden Volume Three. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch; the north arrow is turned slightly left of the page. It adjoins sheet 3 on the left, 12 above and 5 on the right.
notes: Printed sheet number 4; previous edition sheet 8 of volume 2.
South 7th Street is a dual carriageway in OpenStreetMap, about 27 m between the two roadways, with the old PRR line between them; both roadway junctions were used as control.
Roberts, Felton, Edmunds, Blaine and Seward survive only as service streets in OpenStreetMap or not at all and were not used as control.
Berkley Street east of South 7th Street is drawn about 25 m south of Berkley Street west of it; OpenStreetMap shows the same jog.
printed sheet 4 (8 vol 2), 50 ft: PRR electric line on S 7th, Trenton and Newton Avs

canvas-20.description: Sheet 11 covers the centre of South Camden along Broadway, from the railroad at the top to Washington Street at the bottom, between South 5th Street on the left and South 6th Street on the right. The Pennsylvania Railroad's West Jersey and Seashore tracks cross the top, with a retaining wall, a railroad station and a club house on the north side of Mickle Street. Broadway runs down the middle and William Street lies to its west. South of Mickle Street the sheet is more commercial than its neighbours: a movie theatre on Stevens Street, the German Evangelical Lutheran Church and its school, the Camden Veterinary Hospital, a tin shop, the Camden Elbow Co. tin work, a garage for 40 cars, the Fraternal Order of Eagles hall and a bakery. East of Broadway the blocks around the Y.W.C.A. (a reinforced concrete building with a gymnasium) hold the Garden Hotel and the Fuhrman School of Music, and the large block below holds the 1st M.E. Church, the Y.W.C.A. annex, the Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 980 and the American Legion Post 7, each set in its own yard. Rowhouses fill the lower blocks along Washington and Auburn Streets. Chapel Place and Griffee Court are narrow alleys on the left. A curved street edge at the right margin is the bend of South 6th Street. Water mains and street widths of 60 and 66 feet are marked. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch; its north arrow is turned slightly left of the page, and it adjoins sheet 10 on the left, 12 on the right, 18 above and 3 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 11; previous edition sheet 3 of volume 2.
Mickle Street is now Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard, about 50 feet off the drawn line, so its junctions were left out of the control.
South 6th Street in OpenStreetMap bends north-west of Washington Street and does not follow the drawn street; the Stevens Street junction with it was excluded.
William, Auburn, Chapel Place and Griffee Court survive only as service streets in OpenStreetMap or not at all and were not used as control.
printed sheet 11 (3 vol 2), 50 ft: Broadway, Mickle to Washington, YWCA

canvas-26.description: Sheet 15 covers the Delaware River waterfront of downtown Camden between Market Street at the top and Federal Street near the bottom, with Delaware Avenue along the left edge, North and South Front Street in the middle and North and South 2nd Street at the right. Almost the whole sheet belongs to two manufacturers. The Campbell Soup Company holds the large warehouse blocks between Delaware Avenue and North Front Street and the plant on the east side of North Front Street, drawn in fireproof construction with a summer canning factory, an engine house, a water filter plant and warehouses linked across North Front Street by a covered bridge on the second storey. The J. B. Van Sciver Company, furniture manufacturers and interior decorators, occupies the blocks along Arch and Federal Streets, with furniture warehouses, cabinet shops and wood working machinery, and a note below the sheet describes its watchmen, fire pump and private fire brigade. Smaller blocks along Market Street and Taylor Avenue hold stores, garages, offices, a coffee and tea wholesaler and plumbing supply houses, and the Hotel Ridgeway stands at the left end of the Market Street block. George Street is a short alley between the two northern rows of buildings. Brick and fireproof buildings dominate, with a few frame and metal-clad sheds, and street widths of 60 to 80 ft are marked. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 21 above, 19 to the left, 16 to the right and 50 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 15; the previous-edition number printed under it is cut off at the scan edge and reads like 5 Vol. 1 (medium confidence).

Placed from four hand-picked points at water pipe crossings (Market Street at Delaware Avenue, North Front Street and North 2nd Street, and Federal Street at Delaware Avenue); no street junction on the sheet was detected automatically, because Market Street has only its south side drawn and the parcels do not cover the riverfront. Low confidence.

Taylor Avenue and George Street, and the junctions of Federal Street with North Front and North 2nd Street, are not in the modern OpenStreetMap street network; the area is now under the Ben Franklin Bridge approach and the Campbell Soup and Rutgers-Camden sites.
Delaware Avenue is today the heavy boulevard of Jersey Joe Walcott Boulevard and Delaware Avenue; the modern junction centre used for it may differ from the drawn one by several metres.
printed sheet 15, 50 ft: riverfront, Campbell Soup / Van Sciver, Market to Federal; four hand-picked points, low confidence

canvas-28.description: Sheet 16 covers downtown Camden between Market Street at the top and the Pennsylvania Railroad cut with Bridge Avenue at the bottom, and between North and South 2nd Street at the left and North and South 4th Street at the right, with North and South 3rd Street in the middle. The upper half is the commercial core around Market Street and Arch Street: the Campbell Soup Company's cookers and warehouses fill the block between Market and Arch Streets at the left, and across North 3rd Street stand the West Jersey Title and Guaranty Company bank, the Masonic Temple, the Post Office with its annex and Camden Commercial College, the last two shown in unusual colours for their special construction. Carter Alley and Newark Place are narrow service streets in that block. South of Arch Street the Daily Courier press building and the First Spiritualist Church stand on the left, and between Federal Street and Taylor Avenue are rows of stores and dwellings, the Camden Safe Deposit and Trust Company bank, a laundry and an auto showroom. Taylor Avenue is a narrow street behind them. Bridge Avenue and the Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) tracks cross the bottom of the sheet in a wide cut with iron bridge notes. Street widths of 60 to 80 ft are marked, and the water mains of 4 to 12 inches are drawn in each street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 22 above, 17 to the right, 9 below and 15 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 16, previous edition sheet 6 of volume 1.

Taylor Avenue, Carter Alley and Newark Place do not exist as through streets in the modern OpenStreetMap network and were not used as control; Arch Street at North 3rd Street and North 2nd Street, and Federal Street at North 2nd Street, are likewise not junctions today.
Market Street at the top is drawn only on its south side; its junctions with North 3rd and 4th Street are placed from the drawn edge and half the printed width.
printed sheet 16, 50 ft: Market to Federal and Bridge Av, N 2nd to N 4th

canvas-30.description: Sheet 17 covers the downtown Camden blocks between Market Street at the top and the Pennsylvania Railroad tracks at the bottom, and between North and South 4th Street at the left and North 6th Street at the right, with North and South 5th Street in the middle. North of Arch Street is a civic and church district: St. Paul's Episcopal Church with its parish house, the First Baptist Church, a municipal repair shop and garage, the Police Patrol station and the Fire Department with Engine Company No. 2 and Truck Company No. 1, and the Salvation Army, all in the block between North 4th and North 5th Streets. East of North 5th Street are moving picture theatres, a motor truck body builder, the Herman Z. Cutler sheet metal works and the Camden Safety Storage Company, and at the right edge the George Genge Public School. Columbia Street is a narrow street through the right-hand block. South of Arch Street the sheet is mixed commerce: the Central Trust Company, parking lots, the offices of the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey, the Camden Fire Insurance Association, stores and flats, with a long diagonal row of buildings along the line of Federal Street and Hudson Street. Taylor Avenue, Park Place and Hudson Alley are narrow streets behind them. The Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) tracks, platform and iron bridge cross the bottom of the sheet beside Bridge Avenue. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 23 above, 18 to the right, 10 and 11 below and 16 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 17, previous edition sheet 7 of volume 1.
Taylor Avenue, Columbia Street, Park Place and Hudson Alley are not in the modern OpenStreetMap street network and were not used as control.
The Federal Street and North 4th Street junction lies near the binding gutter at the left edge, where the scan curves.
printed sheet 17, 50 ft: Market to Bridge Av, N 4th to N 6th

canvas-32.description: Sheet 18 covers downtown Camden between Market Street at the top and the Pennsylvania Railroad yard at the bottom, from North 6th Street and Hudson Street at the left to North 8th Street and Day Street at the right, with North 7th Street and the diagonal lines of Broadway and Haddon Avenue crossing the middle. The County Court House with its jail, a fireproof building of 1924 with a dome, stands in a walled lot at the left between North 6th Street and Broadway. In the next block stand Immaculate Conception Catholic Church and priests' house, Saint Mary Catholic School, Camden Catholic High School with its gymnasium and auditorium, and a convent, all in blue for their special construction. North-east of North 7th Street are rows of dwellings along Market Street, Roy Street and Carman Street, the Bell Telephone Company's exchange of 1926, and the Camden City Dispensary. South of Federal Street lie the Young Men's Christian Association building and school, the Merchants Trust Company, the Munger and Long department store at the left, rows of dwellings on Carman Street and a large garage. Haddon Avenue runs diagonally across the right-hand blocks, and Bridge Avenue and the broad Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) yard with platforms and sheds fill the bottom. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 24 above, 19 to the right, 11 below and 17 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 18, previous edition sheet 89 of volume 1.
Haddon Avenue is drawn meeting Federal Street about 30 m east of North 7th Street; the modern junction is about 93 m east of it, so Haddon Avenue was left out as control (realigned).
Carman Street and Roy Street are not in the modern OpenStreetMap street network and were not used as control.
printed sheet 18, 50 ft: Market to Bridge Av, Broadway to N 8th; Haddon Av left out (realigned)

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 is the south-east corner of Volume One, a triangular wedge of South Camden between Newton Avenue on the west, the Pennsylvania Railroad's West Jersey and Seashore lines on the east and Line Street on the south. Three diagonal avenues, Newton, Trenton and Haddon, fan out across the sheet, and the narrow blocks between them are filled with long terraces of two and three storey brick dwellings, numbered in the 500s on Newton and Haddon Avenues. South 8th Street cuts across the lower left, and South 9th Street and Silver Street reach Line Street at the bottom. At the lower left stand the Penn Pressed Metal Co. works, with a machine shop and office, and at the bottom right a garage (capacity 22 cars) stands at the corner of Haddon Avenue and Line Street. Along the right edge the sheet is crossed by many tracks of the PRR (W. J. & S. Division), with an iron bridge at the top, and the streets Border and Starr Avenue are drawn beside them. At the top Cartaret Street and School Alley run off the sheet. West Camden streets Berkley and Clinton enter from the left, ending at Newton Avenue. Street widths of 20 to 60 feet are marked and 6, 8, 12 and 30 inch water mains are shown. Much of the sheet is blank paper: the bottom is occupied by the notice See Camden Volume Three. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with a north arrow turned about 15 degrees to the left of the page; it adjoins sheet 4 on the left and 6 on the right.
notes: Printed sheet number 5; the previous-edition number under it is cut off at the left edge of the scan.
The sheet is turned about 15 degrees from the page, more than its neighbours.

Control rests on junctions along Newton Avenue and at Line / South 8th Street only; the Haddon / Line, South 9th Street and Trenton / South 9th Street junctions are in the PRR corridor and could not be measured, so the fit is weakly determined at the east side.
printed sheet 5, 50 ft: wedge between Newton Av, the PRR and Line St, turned about 15 degrees; low confidence

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the ground between Newton Avenue and Starr Avenue in the north-west corner and the Civic Center grounds on the east, south to Line Street at the bottom, where the sheet meets Camden Volume Three. The upper left is taken by the car barns of the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey: a long motor bus barn with capacity for 40 buses, the car barns proper, a paint shop, carpenter shop, repairing and overhauling shop, armature and machine shops, a store room and storage sheds, with a repair storage yard and transfer pit behind them along Border Street. Starr Avenue runs diagonally across the sheet with a railroad siding beside it. Below Starr Avenue, near Line Street, stand the plumbers' supplies warehouses of Fleck Bros. with a siding and concrete platforms, and a public garage with capacity for 150 cars. The eastern half is the open Civic Center Grounds, crossed by park drives, with the Convention Hall at the bottom right, an L-shaped building with an entrance, stage, heater room and ticket booths; its east wing continues onto sheet 8. Water pipes of 6 inches run in the drives and in Line Street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, nearly square to north; it adjoins sheets 13 and 14 at the top left, 7 at the top right, 8 on the right and Volume Three below.
notes: Printed sheet 6.
Placed from three corners of the motor bus repair shop and heater room carried from sheet 13 and a fire alarm box at Line Street carried from sheet 5 (helmert); low confidence.
Starr Avenue follows today's Mount Ephraim Avenue; Border Street no longer exists.
printed sheet 6, 50 ft: Public Service car barns on Starr Av (today Mount Ephraim Av), Civic Center grounds, Convention Hall; placed from points carried from sheets 13 and 5, low confidence

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 shows the southern part of the Civic Center Grounds between the park drive on the left and the Cooper River on the right, south to Line Street at the bottom, where the sheet meets Camden Volume Three; the Cooper River shore and everything east of it belong to Camden Volume Two. Almost the whole sheet is open ground. At the bottom left is the east end of the Convention Hall, continued from sheet 6, and along Line Street stand the works of Mechling Bros. Chemical Co.: a long storage building and a few smaller buildings. A 6 inch water pipe runs in the drive and in Line Street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, with north up; it adjoins sheet 6 on the left and sheet 7 at the top.
notes: Printed sheet 8.
Anchored on the south-east corner of the Convention Hall wing carried from sheet 6, with the atlas scale and the rotation of sheet 6; very low confidence.
printed sheet 8, 50 ft: Civic Center grounds, Cooper River, Mechling Bros. Chemical Co. on Line St; anchored on a point carried from sheet 6, very low confidence

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 covers the blocks between Bridge Avenue at the top and Washington Street at the bottom, from South 2nd Street on the left to South 4th Street at the right edge, with South 3rd Street dividing the sheet. The top is the approach to the Delaware River bridge: Bridge Avenue is drawn 100 feet wide and crossed by the Pennsylvania Railroad's West Jersey and Seashore tracks, with iron bridges over them. Along the railroad, on Mickle Street, stand the P.R.R. Dept. Y.M.C.A., E. Moebus Co. photo printing and C. B. Edwards electric repair shop. South of Mickle Street are blocks of two and three storey dwellings along Stevens, Benson and Washington Streets, with Channing Terrace and Cleveland Terrace (Kent Place) as small interior courts. There is a Baptist church (Colored) and a garage for 120 cars on Stevens Street, a bakery with its oven on South 3rd Street, and the Camden Day Nursery on South 4th Street. At the left, beyond South 2nd Street, is an area of factories: Chas. K. Cook leather goods and S. B. Goff & Sons cough syrup and liniment factory, with a warehouse and small yellow sheds. The bottom margin carries empty block outlines. Water mains of 4 to 16 inches and street widths of 60 and 66 feet are marked. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with a north arrow turned about 7 degrees from the page; the neighbours are sheet 50 on the left, 10 on the right, 16 above and 1 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 9; the previous-edition number under it is cut off at the left edge of the scan.
Mickle Street is now Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard, and the modern line is about 50 feet from the drawn line, so Mickle junctions were left out of the control.
Bridge Avenue is now Admiral Wilson Boulevard.
The right edge of the scan cuts South 4th Street; two junctions on it rest on the drawn edge plus half the street width.
Only about five control points, in two columns, place this sheet; confidence is low to medium.
printed sheet 9, 50 ft: Bridge Av to Washington, S 2nd to S 4th; Mickle St (MLK Blvd) left out as displaced

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 covers the blocks between Bridge Avenue at the top and Washington Street at the bottom, from South 4th Street on the left to South 5th Street on the right, with West Street dividing the sheet and Henry Street running down the lower right. The top is the bridge approach: Bridge Avenue is crossed by the Pennsylvania Railroad's West Jersey and Seashore tracks with iron bridges, and South 5th Street meets it at an angle at top right. Along the railroad on the north side of Mickle Street are the Delaware & Atlantic Telephone Co. (Bell Telephone Co.) exchange, a garage for 60 cars, and a row of small dwellings. South of Mickle Street the blocks hold two and three storey dwellings and some frame buildings, with the Ahav Zedak Synagogue between Stevens and Benson Streets and Shepherd's Hall and a lumber yard east of West Street. The Hitchner & Holmes carpet and trim mill and wall paper storage fills a block at the top right, with Judson Place beside it. Benson Public School, with its annex, stands at the lower left at Benson and Washington Streets. The blocks east of West Street are a dense mixture of brick and frame dwellings with shared courts. Riley Street appears at the bottom, and the blocks beyond Washington Street are blank outlines. Water mains and street widths of 40 to 66 feet are marked. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and its north arrow is turned about 7 degrees; it adjoins sheet 9 on the left, 11 on the right, 17 above and 2 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 10; previous edition sheet 2 of volume 2.
Mickle Street is now Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard, about 50 feet off the drawn line, so its junctions were left out of the control.
Bridge Avenue is now Admiral Wilson Boulevard.
Henry and Riley survive only as service streets in OpenStreetMap or not at all and were not used as control.
printed sheet 10 (2 vol 2), 50 ft: Mickle to Washington, S 4th to S 5th

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers the Cooper Hospital block and the civic buildings of the Haddon Avenue wedge in south-central downtown Camden. The left half is dominated by Cooper Hospital, a campus of connected ward buildings, a kitchen and dining wing, nurses' home, men's dormitory, laundry, laboratory and shop, set in a large rounded-corner block between South 6th Street on the left and the railroad cut that runs diagonally down the centre alongside South 7th Street (labelled P.R.R. W.J. & S. Div.). Below Benson Street lies a block of two- and three-storey dwellings in long terraces between South 6th Street and Chambers Avenue, with a second block of dwellings between Chambers Avenue and South 7th Street, down to Washington Street. The right half is cut by the diagonal Haddon Avenue and Wright Avenue. At the upper right stands the Third Regiment Armory, N.G.N.J., with a drill hall skylight, facing a triangular park with a soldiers' monument; the City Hall, with jail, court and police department wings and a clock and bell tower, stands in the wedge to the south between Haddon Avenue, Washington Street and Trenton Avenue. Cartaret Street runs along the right edge and Mickle Street crosses the top. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are marked in every street, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, with the street grid nearly square to the sheet (north about 2 degrees off vertical), and the adjoining sheets are 19 above, 20 and 14 to the right, 4 below and 5 to the lower left.
notes: Printed sheet number 12, previous edition sheet 4 of volume 2.
Mickle Street west of South 11th Street is now Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard; Mickle and Cartaret are not control streets here.
South 7th Street is drawn as a 75 ft railroad cut; OpenStreetMap carries two ways either side of it, so it was not used as control.
Haddon Avenue is drawn much wider than today's roadway; its junctions were accepted with residuals under 1.7 m.
printed sheet 12 (4 vol 2), 50 ft: Cooper Hospital, armory, Haddon Av wedge

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 covers the ground east of the Pennsylvania Railroad's Amboy Division cut between Federal Street at the top left and the Public Service yards at the bottom, bounded by Wright Avenue on the left and Starr Avenue on the right, with Newton Avenue running down the middle and South 9th Street crossing the sheet below its centre. The railroad cut with several tracks and the Cooper Street and Federal Street crossings fills the top left corner. Along Wright Avenue south of the tracks stand the plant of the American Ice Co., with its engine and boiler house, tank room, delivery room, a fireproof ice storage house built in 1920, and a garage and stable. The large block between Wright and Newton Avenues north of South 9th Street is open ground with a single small shed. East of Newton Avenue the Public Service Corporation of New Jersey has an athletic field with open bleacher seats, a grandstand and dressing room, served by a railroad siding along Starr Avenue. South of South 9th Street are the armory of Battery B, 1st Regiment, N.J. National Guard, with its drill shed and gun shed, and the Public Service Corporation's car storage yards and motor bus repair shop with capacity for 40 buses. Water mains of 6 to 30 inches run in Newton Avenue and Wright Avenue. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch and is turned about 40 degrees, with north toward the upper left; it adjoins sheets 20 and 14 on the left, 27 at the top, 7 on the right and 6 at the bottom right.
notes: Printed sheet 13; previous editions sheet 34 of volume 1 and 67-72 of volume 2.
South 9th Street here is today's South 11th Street (OpenStreetMap), the drawn junction with Newton Avenue matching the modern Newton Avenue / South 11th Street node to about 2 m.
Starr Avenue follows today's Memorial Avenue and Mount Ephraim Avenue.
Placed from two block corners carried from sheet 14 and the detected Newton Avenue / South 11th Street junction (exact three-point fit).
printed sheet 13 (34 vol 1), 50 ft, turned about 40 degrees: American Ice Co., armory, Public Service athletic field; printed S 9th St is today South 11th Street, Starr Av is Memorial Av

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 shows the dwelling blocks and railroad corridor on the south side of Haddon Avenue in Camden, drawn turned about 40 degrees from the usual orientation, so that Wright Avenue and Newton Avenue run up the page and Haddon Avenue, Carteret Street and Trenton Avenue run across it. The lower third is a district of two- and three-storey brick row dwellings between Washington Street on the left and Newton Avenue on the right, in blocks cut by the narrow Blaine and Seward streets, with Trenton Avenue along the bottom and New Street leaving it below. The middle band contains long terraces of dwellings on both sides of Carteret Street and School Alley (Lane), and the Manual Training and High School, a large three-storey brick building with a stage and balcony, on the north side of Haddon Avenue next to Newton Avenue. Above them a broad diagonal corridor of Pennsylvania Railroad tracks (W.J. & S. Division) crosses the page under an iron bridge near Newton Avenue; a long vacant factory building with 28 skylights and hydrant hose connections stands in the open ground to the north, with a small works building near Newton Avenue and Border Street. Auto repair and a few dwellings stand at the left on Wright Avenue. Water pipes of 6 to 30 inches are marked in the streets, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with north pointing toward the upper left, and adjoining sheets are 13 above, 20 and 12 to the left, 6 and 5 to the right and 4 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 14, previous edition sheet 9 of volume 2.
The sheet is turned about 42 degrees from the north-up orientation of its neighbours; the printed north arrow points toward the upper left.
Blaine and Seward survive only as service alleys or not at all in OpenStreetMap and were not used as control; Wright Avenue north of Washington Street was not used.
Control is four street junctions (Haddon, Trenton, Washington, Newton) at the corners of the lower district; the upper corridor and the vacant factory have no control.
printed sheet 14 (9 vol 2), 50 ft, turned about 42 degrees: Haddon, Carteret, Trenton rows, Manual Training and High School

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 covers a district of mixed dwellings, shops and small works in central Camden between Market Street along the top and the Pennsylvania Railroad cut that crosses the lower part of the sheet from lower left to upper right. Market Street is lined along its south side with a continuous row of two- and three-storey brick stores and dwellings from North 8th Street to the diagonal South 8th Street, including the Second Spiritualist Church near the left end. Federal Street, drawn at a slant, runs below it, with a block of brick-filled lots and detached dwellings between the two streets. The middle of the sheet holds the blocks between Federal Street, Carman Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, cut by the narrow Fogarty Avenue and a drive, with dwellings, a large garage with a cement floor for twenty cars, a printing office and sheds. At the lower left Haddon Avenue crosses the railroad cut, with a battery station, a stone cutting works (Wm. Lamont, with power and gasoline engine) and a polishing and cutting shop beside it. The railroad (P.R.R., W.J. & S. Division) is drawn in a wide retained cut with a foot-of-slope line and crossings by Warren Avenue and South 7th Street; below it a wedge of dwellings sits between the cut and Mickle Street, and a gasoline station stands in open ground. Water pipes of 3 to 30 inches are marked with their sizes in the streets, with hydrants. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 13 degrees from the sheet edges; adjoining sheets are 25 above, 18 to the left, 20 to the right and 11, 12 and 8 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 19, volume 1; the previous-edition number printed under it is cut off by the scan edge.
Market Street and North 10th Street are the only modern junction on the sheet; the rest of this district was cleared for the Ben Franklin Bridge approach and I-676.
Mickle Street here is now part of Doctor Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard; Fogarty Avenue is read from a small label and is medium confidence.
Placement rests on one hand-picked point (Market and North 10th, from the drawn Market north edge plus half of 80 ft) with the scale and a 13 degree rotation assumed: low confidence.
printed sheet 19, 50 ft: Market/Federal/Carman district and railroad cut; anchored on one hand pick, low confidence

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 shows the railroad corridor and the dwelling blocks south of Market and Federal Streets, at the Warren Avenue approach to the Camden terminal district. The Pennsylvania Railroad cut (P.R.R. Amboy Division, with a W.J. & S. line curving through the lower left behind a stone retaining wall) runs diagonally from the lower left to the top right under steel and iron bridges at South 8th Street and South 9th Street. Above it, between Market, Federal and Bridge Avenue, are rows of two- and three-storey brick dwellings numbered 800 to 846 on the north side of Bridge Avenue, with a block of small houses and a store at the end of Federal Street near the top right corner. South of the cut the upper-left blocks are blank, belonging to neighbouring sheets. At the lower left a dense block of brick dwellings fronts Warren Avenue and Carteret Street, behind a curved stone retaining wall twenty feet high, with a dwelling group at the foot of Mickle Street. The large open area at the right holds Wright Avenue, a diagonal street, and South 9th Street crossing it, with a coal yard (Geo. B. Newton and Co.) and a long curved coal pockets building 30 feet high beside a siding. Water pipes of 4 to 30 inches are marked, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 13 degrees from the sheet edges; adjoining sheets are 26 above, 19 to the left, 13 to the right and 12 and 14 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 20, previous edition sheet 10-34 of volume 1.
Market Street and North 10th Street are the only modern junction on the sheet; the district was cleared for the Ben Franklin Bridge approach and I-676.
Placement rests on one hand-picked point (Market and North 10th, from the drawn Market north edge plus half of 80 ft) with the scale and a 13 degree rotation assumed: low confidence.
The OpenStreetMap Federal Street sits about 10 m off the drawn one at the left of the sheet, which may point to a rotation error of a few degrees.
printed sheet 20, 50 ft: railroad corridor, Warren and Wright Avs; anchored on one hand pick, low confidence

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 covers the north-west corner of downtown Camden between Linden Street at the top and Market Street at the bottom, and between Delaware Avenue at the left and North 2nd Street at the right, with Point Street and North Front Street running up the page between them. The sheet belongs to two firms. In the upper blocks the Campbell Soup Company has a long brick and yellow-roofed factory beside Delaware Avenue, with dwelling rows on the blocks to the east along Linden Street and Penn Street. At the upper right the Standard Tank and Seat Company and the Celluloid Manufacturing Company stand around Centennial Avenue. The rest of the sheet is the Victor Talking Machine Company: its fireproof veneer, cutting and warehouse buildings along Delaware Avenue, an office building and auditorium and a lunch club on North Front Street, the Cooper Branch Public Library standing in a large open square, and below Cooper Street the manufacturing, record pressing, cabinet shops and shipping departments covering four blocks down to Market Street, with covered bridges across Cooper Street and North Front Street and a tunnel under it. Ambler Street and Point Street are narrow streets through the dwelling blocks. The 1st National State Bank of Camden stands at the lower right on Market Street. Water mains of 6 to 18 inches are drawn in every street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 29 above, 22 to the right, 15 below and 48 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 21, previous edition sheet 11 of volume 1.
Ambler Street and Centennial Avenue are not in the modern OpenStreetMap street network and were not used as control.
The left edge of the sheet is curved into the binding gutter around Delaware Avenue.
printed sheet 21, 50 ft: Linden to Market, Delaware Av to N 2nd; Campbell Soup and Victor works

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 covers downtown Camden between Linden Street at the top and Market Street at the bottom, and between North 2nd Street at the left and North 4th Street at the right, with Friends Avenue and North 3rd Street in the middle. Rows of three-storey brick dwellings and apartment houses line Linden, Penn, Wilson and Lawrence Streets, and several apartment buildings carry names: Sabra Apartments, Cades Apartments, Benjamin Apartments, the Kinney Apartments and Helene Apartments. The Hotel Camden stands on North 2nd Street at the left and the Camden Club at the corner of North 3rd Street. Churches are numerous: the North Baptist Church with its dome, gymnasium and Sunday school at the top right, the First Church of Christ Scientist on North 3rd Street between Penn and Cooper Streets and again below Cooper Street on North 3rd Street, and another church near the Hotel Camden. Market Street along the bottom is built up with stores, offices and a bakery, among them the Security Trust Company bank and the Solomon Building, with garages and an alley court on the lower left. Marley Place is a short alley at the right. The streets are marked 60 ft, Cooper Street 100 ft and Market Street 80 ft, and water mains of 3 to 16 inches are drawn in each. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 30 above, 23 to the right, 16 below and 21 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 22, previous edition sheet 12 of volume 1.

Penn Street between North 2nd and North 5th Street, Wilson Street, Lawrence Street, Friends Avenue and Marley Place no longer exist in the modern OpenStreetMap street network; only Market, Cooper and North 2nd to 4th Street junctions were used as control.
Cooper Street meets North 4th Street at two modern nodes 67 m apart; the eastern one (39.94714, -75.12204) was used and the western one excluded.
printed sheet 22, 50 ft: Linden to Market, N 2nd to N 4th

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 shows central Camden between North 4th Street, in the binding gutter at the left edge, and North 6th Street at the right, from Linden Street at the top to Market Street at the bottom. Penn, Lawrence and Cooper Streets cross it, with the narrow Rex Place and Marley Place. The two northern blocks are mostly two-storey brick rowhouses in long terraces with their rear yards and outbuildings; the upper right corner is open ground traversed by a faint diagonal line for the bridge approach, and Belview Private Hospital stands at the top of North 5th Street. Mt. Presbyterian Church occupies much of the block between North 5th and North 6th Streets above Penn Street. South of Cooper Street the character turns commercial: Centenary M.E. Church and a Masonic Temple with an auditorium and banquet room stand on the left of North 5th Street, and Trinity Baptist Church, a garage for about twenty cars, an auto show room and the Chamber of Commerce line the right side, with offices and stores along Market Street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Water pipes of 4 to 8 inches are drawn in the streets, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. Adjoining sheets are 31 above, 24 to the right, 17 below, and the sheet to the left lies beyond the gutter; the printed margin gives the previous edition as 13, Volume 1.
notes: Printed sheet number 23, previous edition sheet 13 of volume 1.
Market Street here is drawn narrower than its modern width (80 to 95 ft in the parcels); the two Market Street control points are boundary points and carry the most uncertainty.

Lawrence Street, Rex Place and Marley Place are not in the modern street network used as control; North 4th Street was left out because its Cooper Street node is doubled in OpenStreetMap and lies in the gutter.
Part of the upper right corner is the approach to the Delaware River Bridge (now the Benjamin Franklin Bridge); the line is faint on this sheet.
printed sheet 23, 50 ft: Linden to Market, N 4th to N 6th

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 covers the area west of the Camden end of the Delaware River Bridge, between North 6th Street at the left and North 8th Street at the right, from Linden Street at the top to Market Street at the bottom, with Penn, Lawrence and Cooper Streets across it. The upper left is a large open area lettered Bridge Plaza, with only a few buildings on the Penn Street block. The upper right is built up with rowhouses and dwellings along North 7th and North 8th Streets, cut off at the top by the diagonal right of way of a railroad running from upper left to lower right. Broadway runs obliquely through the lower left and bears the larger commercial buildings: the Walt Whitman Hotel, the Elks Club home (B.P.O. Elks) beside it, the Wilson Building, and the Stanley Theatre with vaudeville and motion pictures at the Market Street corner. Epiphany Evangelical Lutheran Church, a Friends school and meeting house, a school and the Drake Hall building stand in the lower right. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Water pipes with sizes, hydrants and fire alarm boxes are drawn in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 32 above, 23 to the left, 25 to the right and 18 below; the printed margin gives the previous edition as 14, Volume 1.
notes: Printed sheet number 24, previous edition sheet 14 of volume 1.
The sheet is controlled by only four points: three along Cooper Street and one hand-picked pipe crossing at Penn and North 6th Streets. Treat it as low confidence.
Market Street was left out of the control: it is drawn narrower than its modern right of way and its junctions disagreed by several metres.
Bridge Plaza is the open plaza at the Camden end of the Delaware River Bridge, now the Benjamin Franklin Bridge; most of it is blank on this sheet.
printed sheet 24, 50 ft: Bridge Plaza, N 6th to N 8th; Market St left out (widened), low confidence

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 shows the blocks between North 8th Street at the left edge and North 10th Street at the right, from Linden Street at the top to Market Street at the bottom, crossed by Kimber Street, Penn Street, Lawrence Street, Cooper Alley, Cooper Street and Carpenter Street. The upper two thirds are solid rowhouse blocks: long terraces of two-storey brick dwellings with small rear outbuildings face each other across the cross streets, with Bethany M.E. Church on the east side of North 9th Street near Cooper Alley. A railroad cuts diagonally from the upper left to the lower right across the sheet, running through the middle of the lower half. West of it, south of Cooper Street, stand the plant of the R. M. Hollingshead Co., a ware house, private garage and offices, and the Supplee-Wills-Jones Dairies at Carpenter Street; east of it the R. M. Hollingshead Co. also occupies a triangular block of oils, greases and soaps works, with rowhouses to the east. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Water pipes of 4 to 6 inches are drawn in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 33 above, 24 to the left, 26 to the right and 19 below; the printed margin gives the previous edition as 15, Volume 1.
notes: Printed sheet number 25, previous edition sheet 15 of volume 1.

Control is thin: two detected points on North 10th Street and Linden Street, one on Linden at North 9th and a hand-picked pipe crossing at Penn and North 9th Street. Cooper Street, Kimber and Lawrence do not connect to the numbered streets in the modern network. Low confidence.
The Linden Street row is drawn on its south edge only; the junctions are boundary points placed half the street width beyond the drawn edge.
printed sheet 25, 50 ft: N 8th to N 10th, rail diagonal; low confidence

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 shows the eastern end of the central Camden grid, where the regular blocks along North 10th and North 11th Streets meet a wedge of diagonal streets running to the south east. Linden, Penn, Lawrence, Cooper, Carpenter and Federal Streets cross it, with Chester and Summit Streets between Linden and Penn, Richman Alley, and Bridge Blvd, a wide blank right of way that runs east from Penn Street. West of North 11th Street the blocks are mostly two-storey brick rowhouses in uniform terraces, with a row of small blue-coloured buildings and a few garages; the lower left corner is occupied by a large factory and ware house block on the Carpenter and Market Street corner. East of North 11th Street the blocks are cut by the diagonals: the Richard W. Jefferis Co. metal furniture works and a private garage lie along the Linden Street diagonal, St. Stephens Episcopal Church stands beside Lawrence Street, and rowhouses fill the long wedge between Cooper Street and Federal Street, which closes to a point at the right. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 34 above, 25 to the left, 27 to the right and 20 below; the printed margin gives the previous edition as 16, 33 and 34, Volume 1.
notes: Printed sheet number 26, previous edition sheets 16, 33 and 34 of volume 1.

Control comes from four junctions on the regular grid at the left; the diagonal streets to the east (Linden, Penn, Lawrence, Cooper, Federal) have no surviving modern line and carry no control. Bridge Blvd. is the present Admiral Wilson Boulevard. Low confidence for the east side.
The left edge is curved by the binding gutter, so the two North 10th Street points carry the largest residuals.
printed sheet 26, 50 ft: N 10th to N 11th and diagonal wedge to Bridge Blvd; east side uncontrolled, low confidence

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 covers the Cooper River shore of north-central Camden at the east end of the downtown grid, where the Bridge Boulevard approach crosses the open ground along the river. At the left, North 12th Street runs down the sheet with blocks of dwellings and small works to its west: terraces of brick dwellings on Linden, Penn and Lawrence Streets (numbered 1163 to 1197), the Mount Carmel Baptist Church with a light and electric fund building, a block of auto houses, a lumber shed, a shavings house, woodworking and auto repair shops near Cooper Street and the Federal Street corner. East of North 12th Street a long triangular block holds a row of six dwellings numbered 210 to 232 beside a concrete driveway. A large vacant factory with several buildings (walls pilastered, raised sidelight, with a separate small building) stands at the top beside the Cooper River, drawn with its shoreline and boat houses at the upper left, with a vacant store and warehouse buildings near the bank. Bridge Boulevard, a very wide street, crosses the right-hand side diagonally. The Pennsylvania Railroad (Amboy Division) runs through the lower right on steel bridges over Bridge Boulevard and a concrete bridge over Federal Street, with a city pump house, an oil house and a storage building along it. The upper right of the sheet is marked See Camden Volume Two. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, turned about 11 degrees from north; adjoining sheets are 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 to the left, 28 to the right and 13 and 3 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 27, previous edition sheet 33-34-35 of volume 1.
Bridge Blvd. is the approach now called Admiral Wilson Boulevard; Penn, Lawrence and Linden survive only west of North 12th Street.

Placed from the Penn Street and North 12th Street crossing (hand-picked from the water pipes) with scale and rotation from the configuration; the Lawrence and North 12th crossing agrees with it to 2.4 m. Low confidence.
printed sheet 27, 50 ft: N 12th Street to the Cooper River; anchored on Penn / N 12th, low confidence

sheet-29.description: Sheet 29 covers the North Camden waterfront blocks near the Delaware River between Delaware Avenue at the left edge and North 2nd Street at the right, from Vine Street at the top to Linden Street at the bottom, crossed by Elm and Pearl Streets, with Point Street and North Front Street running north and south. The district is industrial. Atlas Plywood Corp. and its lumber pile occupy the upper left; the Camden Foundry Co., with iron foundry, pattern and machine shops, fills the left side of Elm Street; the West Jersey Paper Mfg. Co. stands at Danenhower Street. A wide strip across the middle of the sheet is the elevated approach to the bridge, drawn as two long curved lines that cross Point Street and North Front Street. Below it the Victor Talking Machine Co. fills the block between Pearl and Linden Streets with its printing department and record manufacturing buildings, and H. Humphreys & Co. have a lumber yard with sheds at the lower left. Dwellings in rows occupy the right-hand blocks along North 2nd Street, with England Place and Birch Street between them, and Main Street appears in the top right corner. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Water pipes are drawn in most streets. Adjoining sheets are 35 and 36 above, 30 to the right and 21 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 29; the previous edition number in the margin is cut off and was not read.

The Victor Talking Machine Co. block, the foundry and the elevated bridge approach cover most junctions in the middle of the sheet, so Linden/Point, Linden/North Front and Pearl/North Front were not detected.
Danenhower Street is spelled with an n on the sheet; OpenStreetMap has Danehower Street. North Front is lettered 'N. FRONT'; no suffix was read.
The elevated approach to the Delaware River Bridge (now the Benjamin Franklin Bridge) crosses the middle of the sheet.
Delaware Avenue is lettered on the left edge in the binding gutter and was not used as control.
printed sheet 29, 50 ft: Vine to Linden, Point to N 2nd, waterfront industry

sheet-30.description: Sheet 30 covers North Camden between North 2nd Street at the left and North 4th Street at the right, from Vine Street at the top to Linden Street at the bottom, crossed by Main, Cedar, Elm, Birch, Pearl and Cole Streets. A broad diagonal belt running from upper left to lower right carries the railroad along Main Street, with its tracks drawn as parallel lines; the blocks on either side are cut to triangles. In the upper blocks rows of two- and three-storey brick dwellings face Elm and Cedar Streets, with Fire Department Engine Co. No. 4 and a wagon shed on Cedar Street and a garage and offices on the triangular block between Cedar and Main. A second broad strip across the middle of the sheet, lettered Elevated Approach to Bridge, runs from the left and curves up to the right; it leaves the central blocks blank. In the lower half are Calvary Presbyterian Church at the left on North 2nd Street, the Grant School and the Cooper School beside Friends Avenue, rows of dwellings along Cole Street, and the Linden Apts. at the right edge. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid turned about 15 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 36 and 37 above, 29 to the left, 31 to the right and 22 below; the printed margin gives the previous edition as 18, Volume 1.
notes: Printed sheet number 30, previous edition sheet 18 of volume 1.
Danenhower is spelled with an n on the sheet; OpenStreetMap has Danehower Street.

The elevated approach to the Delaware River Bridge (now the Benjamin Franklin Bridge) crosses the sheet and covers the old Pearl Street line; Friends Avenue is a service way in OpenStreetMap and was not used.
Two of the seven control points (Vine Street with North 3rd and North 4th Streets) are boundary points on the top edge.
printed sheet 30, 50 ft: Vine to Linden, N 2nd to N 4th, Main St rail

sheet-31.description: Sheet 31 covers North Camden between Vine Street at the top and Linden Street at the bottom, and from North 4th Street in the binding gutter on the left to North 6th Street on the right, with North 5th Street running down the middle. The upper half, between Vine and Elm Streets, is solid rowhouse blocks of two- and three-storey brick dwellings with narrow service alleys and a few small stores and auto houses, with a fire alarm box at Cedar Street. Below Elm Street the Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) crosses the sheet diagonally from upper left to lower right beside Main Street, cutting the blocks into triangles; a large garage for 50 cars and an electric garage with an office stand between North 5th and North 6th Streets north of the tracks. South of Pearl Street the Delaware River Bridge and its approach are drawn as a wide blank swathe with the bridge lines running diagonally, leaving only a small row of dwellings at the lower left and a few lots along Fulton Place and North 6th Street. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, the street grid is turned about 14 degrees from north, and the left edge is curved into the binding gutter. Water pipes are lettered in every street. Adjoining sheets are 37 above, 32 to the right and 23 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 31, previous edition sheet 19 of volume 1.
Cedar, Birch and Fulton Place are not control streets here; the drawn blocks around the Delaware River Bridge approach and the Pennsylvania Railroad no longer match modern streets.
Three control points on North 6th Street (Vine, Pearl and Linden) were hand picked at water-pipe crossings; the left edge curves into the binding gutter and points there carry the largest residuals.
The modern Pearl Street / North 5th Street node 95 m south of the drawn crossing was excluded.
printed sheet 31, 50 ft: bridge approach and PRR diagonal, N 4th to N 6th

sheet-32.description: Sheet 32 covers six rows of North Camden blocks between Vine Street at the top and Linden Street at the bottom, from North 6th Street at the left edge to North 8th Street at the right, with North 7th Street in the middle. Most blocks are lined with two- and three-storey brick dwellings in uniform terraces with alleys between them. The Northeast School stands in the top left block with a portable school house and toilet. Industry lies in the block between Birch and Pearl Streets: Camden Dye Works, J. Husson's works, and the Myers Mfg. Co. box and metal works, with a garage at North 7th Street. South of Pearl Street the Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) enters at the left with a coal bin trestle, and rowhouses fill the blocks below it down to Linden Street. Fern Street cuts the lower right blocks. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from north, and the left edge curves into the binding gutter. Adjoining sheets are 38 above, 33 to the right, 31 to the left and 24 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 32, previous edition sheet 20 of volume 1.
Fern Street is drawn but has no modern junction with the control streets and was not used.
North 6th Street points at the left edge lie in the binding gutter and carry the largest residuals.
printed sheet 32, 50 ft: Vine to Linden, N 6th to N 8th

sheet-33.description: Sheet 33 covers North Camden from Vine Street at the top to Linden Street at the bottom, and from North 8th Street at the left to North 10th Street at the right, with North 9th Street in the middle. It is almost entirely rowhouse blocks of two- and three-storey brick dwellings, with long frontages numbered in the 400s to 900s. Short side streets run through some blocks, Willard and Linwood Streets in the upper left and Ray and Borton Streets in the centre right. Hanson's Bakery with its ovens and wagon shed stands between Cedar and Elm Streets west of North 10th Street, and the Linden Baptist Church with its Bible School occupies the lower middle block at Linden Street. The Inasmuch Mission appears at the foot of the block above Elm Street. Water pipes of 4 to 6 inches run in the streets. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from north. Adjoining sheets are 39 above, 34 to the right, 32 to the left and 25 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 33, previous edition sheet 21 of volume 1.
Willard, Linwood, Ray and Borton are alleys or short streets with no modern junction and were not used as control.
printed sheet 33, 50 ft: Vine to Linden, N 8th to N 10th

sheet-34.description: Sheet 34 is the eastern edge of volume one, where Camden meets the Cooper River. The upper left holds the leather works of Max Bernstein and Son, wool pullers and tanners, and the Bill Rose Leather Co., Inc., a large complex of warehouses, drying and wool rooms, pickling and sulphide rooms and storage sheds along the river bank, with a separate engine and boiler house and coal bunker. Below them is open ground, then a long vacant strip along the north side of Pearl Street, then blocks with the Linden School house and annex at the lower left and empty lots on the west side of North 11th Street, a street shown 30 ft wide. The Cooper River, drawn in blue, crosses the sheet diagonally and is lettered with the note See Camden Volume Two, since the far bank lies in that volume. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from north, and the left edge curves into the binding gutter. Adjoining sheets are 40 above, 33 to the left and 26 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 34, previous edition sheets 22-33 of volume 1.
Georeferenced from one hand-picked point (Linden Street / North 11th Street) with scale and rotation taken from the neighbouring sheets, so the placement is low confidence.
North 11th Street is drawn 30 ft wide.
Sheet 34 shows the Cooper River bank; the opposite bank is blank ground of Volume Two.
printed sheet 34, 50 ft: Cooper River edge, tannery; anchored on Linden / N 11th, low confidence

sheet-35.description: Sheet 35 covers the Cooper Point waterfront district of north Camden between Erie Street at the top and Vine Street at the bottom, from Delaware Avenue and Beach Street at the left to North Front Street at the right, with Point Street running diagonally through the middle. The upper blocks hold rowhouses, with the McNeely Co. glazed kid factory and a chemical store at North Street and Point Street. The middle blocks between York and Wood Streets are mixed dwellings, shops, a tin shop and a bottling works, and the Public Service Corp. of New Jersey transformer house stands at State Street. A large vacant block lies east of Point Street. The lower third is the Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) yard with Taylor Bro's Cooper Point Elevator and a grain and feed store, drawn with many tracks converging toward the right edge. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from north, and the left edge curves into the binding gutter. Adjoining sheets are 41 above, 36 to the right and 47 and 29 below.
notes: Previous edition sheet number not legible on the reduced image.
Delaware Avenue was realigned along the river and the Delaware Avenue / State Street and Erie junctions were not matched; Delaware Avenue / Vine and York were used.
Streets inside the railroad yard are not used as control.
printed sheet 35, 50 ft: Cooper Point elevator and PRR yard, Erie to Vine

sheet-36.description: Sheet 36 covers north Camden from Erie Street at the top to Vine Street at the bottom, between North Front Street at the left and North 3rd Street on the right, with North 2nd Street in the middle. Most blocks are rowhouses with numbered frontages in the 100s to 900s. S. Feather and Co., a mill and manufactory of silk and yarns with a garage, fills the upper left block at Erie Street and North Front Street. The J. M. Cassady Public School and its grounds occupy the block between Grant and State Streets east of North 2nd Street. The lower right block between Larch and Vine Streets has a movie house and a shoe polish manufactory. In the lower left Main Street and the Pennsylvania Railroad (West Jersey and Seashore Division) cross diagonally with yard tracks beyond. Howard, Bailey, Grant and Larch Streets are narrow cross streets. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from north. Adjoining sheets are 42 above, 37 to the right, 35 to the left and 30 and 29 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 36, previous edition sheet 25 of volume 1.
Bailey, Howard, Grant and Larch survive only as service alleys or not at all and were not used as control.
The North Front Street / Vine Street junction was excluded because the railroad yard distorts it (7 m residual).
printed sheet 36, 50 ft: Erie to Vine, N Front to N 3rd, Cassady School

sheet-37.description: Sheet 37 covers six blocks of the North Camden rowhouse district between Erie Street at the top and Vine Street at the bottom, and between North 3rd Street on the left (in the binding gutter) and North 5th Street on the right, with North 4th Street running down the middle. The cross streets are Erie, York, State and Vine, with the narrow alleys Bailey, Grant and Larch between them. Almost every block is lined with two-storey brick dwellings in long uniform terraces along the cross streets, with three-storey rows on the south side of State Street between North 4th and North 5th Streets; corner stores mark several of the corners, and small private garages and auto houses stand along the alleys. The block between North 3rd and North 4th Streets south of Grant Street is more mixed, with detached three-storey dwellings and some open lots. Named buildings are few: Grace Lutheran Church on the west side of North 4th Street at Larch Street, a chemical laboratory and tin shop at North 3rd Street and Grant Street, an auto repair shop on Grant Street and a plumbing shop on Vine Street. Water pipes of 4 to 16 inches with their sizes are drawn in every street, with hydrants and fire alarm boxes, and street widths are marked (60 ft for the numbered streets and for Erie, York and Vine, 70 ft for State Street, 20 to 30 ft for the alleys). The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch, with the street grid turned about 13 degrees from true north; adjoining sheets are 43 above, 38 to the right, 30 and 31 below and 36 to the left.
notes: Printed sheet number 37, previous edition sheet 26 of volume 1.
Bailey, Grant and Larch survive only as service alleys in OpenStreetMap (Bailey Street, Grant Street, Larch Street) and were not used as control.
The left edge of the sheet is curved into the binding gutter around North 3rd Street; points there carry the largest residuals.
printed sheet 37 (26 vol 1), 50 ft: Erie to Vine, N 3rd to N 5th; pilot

sheet-38.description: Sheet 38 covers twelve blocks of the North Camden rowhouse district, drawn at 50 ft to an inch, between Erie Street at the top and Vine Street at the bottom. North 6th Street runs down the middle of the sheet and North 7th Street along the right edge, with the left edge falling near North 5th Street. The cross streets are Erie, York, State and Vine, with the narrow Bailey, Grant and Larch streets between them, and their widths are marked (60 ft for the numbered streets and for Erie, York and Vine). Almost every block is lined with two-storey brick dwellings in long terraces facing the cross streets, with three-storey rows on parts of State and Vine Streets, small private garages and auto houses in the rear lots, and a few corner stores. The most prominent buildings are the John S. Read Public School on the left between Bailey and York Streets, and the State Street M. E. Church, a large brick building with a balcony and a parsonage, on the north side of State Street west of North 6th Street. Water pipes of 4 to 16 inches are shown in the streets with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The sheet is turned so that the street grid is about 13 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 44 above, 39 to the right, 31 below and 32 below right.
notes: Printed sheet number 38, previous edition sheet 27 of volume 1.
Bailey, Grant and Larch survive only as service alleys in OpenStreetMap and were not used as control.
Street names read on the overview-scale image, not on 1:1 crops; medium confidence on the alley names.
printed sheet 38, 50 ft: Erie to Vine, N 6th to N 7th

sheet-39.description: Sheet 39 shows eleven blocks of North Camden between Erie Street at the top and Vine Street at the bottom, and between North 7th Street at the left edge (in the binding gutter) and North 9th Street near the right edge, with North 8th Street running down the middle. It is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 13 degrees from true north. Most blocks are two-storey brick dwelling rows, with three-storey rows near State Street. The upper right block between Erie and Bailey Streets is taken by Pinco Papers Inc., a coating and finishing works with its own engine room and fire alarm box, and the Elexitallic Gasket Co. stands to its west beside a 15 ft alley. In the lower left, between Grant and State Streets, are the C. Howard Hunt Pen Company factory and the Paper Box Mfg. Co., with a machine shop and storage buildings. The W. J. Sewell Public School stands at the lower left near Vine Street. Several narrow lanes are lettered: Duke Alley, Binker Alley, Raymond Street, Willard Street and Linwood Street. Water pipes up to 30 inches are marked on State Street. A compass rose in the upper right margin shows north tilted to the right. Adjoining sheets are 45 above, 38 to the left, 40 to the right, 32 below left and 33 below right.
notes: Printed sheet number 39, previous edition sheet 28 of volume 1.
Bailey, Grant, Duke, Raymond and the other lanes survive only as service ways or not at all in OpenStreetMap and were not used as control.
Detected junctions along the left edge carry larger residuals because the scan curves into the binding gutter.
Street names read on the overview-scale image; the lane names (Duke, Raymond, Willard, Linwood) are medium confidence.
printed sheet 39, 50 ft: Erie to Vine, N 7th to N 9th

sheet-40.description: Sheet 40 lies along the east side of North Camden and reaches the Cooper River. It is drawn at 50 ft to an inch. The left third of the sheet shows rows of two- and three-storey dwellings along North 9th Street and between York Street and Moore Street, and the Highland Worsted Mills occupy the middle, a large complex of lettered factory buildings (Mill A to N, warehouses, repair shop, boiler house with a blue-tinted fire-proof section) between Moore Street and East State Street. A further two blocks of brick dwellings fill the area between East State Street and Vine Street, bounded on the right by North 10th Street. Open ground at the top between Erie Street and York Street is marked as lot 2. The right two-thirds of the sheet is the Cooper River, labelled as continuing on Volume Two, crossed at East State Street by an iron draw bridge. Part of the Camden shore across the river and a lot at lower right belong to the next sheet. A compass rose is placed over the water. Adjoining sheets are 45 above, 39 to the left, 33 below left and 34 below right. The mill complex and the drawbridge approach occupy ground that has since been rebuilt.
notes: Printed sheet number 40, previous edition sheet 32 of volume 1.
Only four junctions were detected; North 9th Street and York Street was hand-picked at the gutter edge. Fit is low confidence.
The drawn scale fits about 2 percent larger than the atlas average.
East State Street east of the bridge is State Street in modern data.
printed sheet 40, 50 ft: strip along the Cooper River, Highland Worsted Mills

sheet-41.description: Sheet 41 shows the Camden waterfront at the north end of the city, where the Delaware River bounds the sheet on the west and north. Erie Street crosses the bottom of the sheet and North Front Street runs up the right-hand side, with Point Street and Beach Street meeting Erie Street near the lower left. Most of the land is given over to boatbuilding and ship repair. The Quigley & Dorp ship and engine builders occupy the shore on the left, with a print shop, lumber storage, machine shop, blacksmith shop and storage sheds, and the Mathis Yacht Building Co. holds the larger yard to the east, with its boat shop, wood working shop, machine shop, lumber shed, storage and supplies buildings, and a number of small outbuildings. Several finger piers and a marine railway (marked as ways) project into the river, drawn in dashed outline where they are wooden piers on piling, and a wide pier with filled earth is marked along the river's edge on the right. A long wooden pier on piling crosses the left edge of the sheet. The shore is drawn with a blue tint and the river is lettered across the sheet. The land south of Erie Street is mostly open, with a few dwellings and the corner of the next sheet's blocks. Water pipes with sizes and street widths (60 ft for Erie Street and North Front Street, 50 ft for Point Street) are lettered in the streets. The sheet is drawn at 50 ft to an inch with the street grid turned about 14 degrees from true north. Adjoining sheets are 42 to the right, 46 below left and 35 below.
notes: The previous-edition sheet number printed under the sheet number is cut off in the binding gutter.

Placed from one measured junction (Erie Street at North Front Street) and one point carried from sheet 35 (the water-pipe corner of Point Street and Erie Street); scale and rotation agree with the 50 ft scale bar and the grid of the neighbouring sheets.
Point Street north of York Street and Beach Street are not in OpenStreetMap as drawn here; modern Point Street stops short of Erie Street and is not used as control.
Most of the waterfront shown here has been rebuilt (Ben Franklin Bridge approach, Campbell Soup and later waterfront redevelopment).
printed sheet 41, 50 ft: waterfront yacht yards; two points, low confidence; Point St left out (displaced)

sheet-42.description: Sheet 42 shows the Delaware River waterfront at the north end of Camden between North Front Street at the left and North 3rd Street near the right edge, and from Erie Street at the bottom upwards. The left half is dominated by the Jersey Leather Co. tannery and the John R. Evans Co. leather works along North 2nd Street, with the Varoma Corp. factory, storage and machine shops near Erie Street. Further buildings along the west side are labelled as manufacturing, tan house and ware houses, with concrete floors. A row of dwellings lies along Segal Street at the lower left. The right half of the sheet is open ground at the river edge with Reed's Ship Repairing, small sheds, a repair shop and the Camden Yacht Club pier. At the lower right are five short blocks of two-storey brick dwellings, with their lots lettered, between Burns, Milton and Byron Streets, which are only 30 ft wide. The shore line forms the top of the sheet with the Delaware River lettered above. Water pipes of 6 inches are drawn in all streets. Adjoining sheets are 36 below, 43 to the right and 41 above.
notes: Printed sheet number 42, previous edition sheet 30 of volume 1.
Low confidence: two points only (Byron and Erie at North 2nd Street) plus one derived; the placement is anchored at the configured scale.
North 3rd Street is drawn about 15 m east of its modern line (the pipe at North 3rd Street is 383 ft from North 2nd against 335 ft in OpenStreetMap), so it was left out as control.
Burns, Milton and Segal survive only as service ways or not at all in OpenStreetMap.
printed sheet 42, 50 ft: riverfront mills; anchored, N 3rd St left out (drawn about 15 m east of modern), low confidence

sheet-43.description: Sheet 43 covers the riverfront north of Erie Street between North 3rd Street at the left and North 5th Street near the right. It is drawn at 50 ft to an inch. Most of the area is undeveloped land: a very large vacant block between Milton Street and the river bounded by North 3rd and North 4th Streets, and a smaller one to the right with the Delaware River shoreline curving through it. Two blocks of two-storey brick dwellings with lettered lots lie at the lower left between Milton, Byron and Erie Streets. In the lower right, the Kind and Knox Gelatin Works occupies a fire-proof building with ice and tank rooms, with a tank room and warehouse, the Peerless Pearl Co. (a pearl button works), a private garage and a row of dwellings along Erie Street. J. C. Vanderslice, ship builder and painter, has yards at the shore, with a boat storage, a print shop and a wooden pier. The Delaware River is lettered twice. A compass rose appears at the upper right. Adjoining sheets are 42 to the left, 44 to the right and 37 below.
notes: Printed sheet number 43.
Four junctions detected (North 4th and North 5th at Erie and Byron); the fit is low confidence (no leave-one-out).
printed sheet 43, 50 ft: riverfront, Erie and Byron; N 3rd St left out, low confidence

sheet-44.description: Sheet 44 shows the Pyne Point waterfront at the northern end of Camden, between North 6th Street at the centre and North 7th Street at the right edge, with Erie Street at the bottom and the Delaware River at the top. It is drawn at 50 ft to an inch. The right half is Pyne Point Park, with a playground, a band stand, a play house, a bath house and a concrete swimming pool near the top. The left half has the Camden Ship Building Co. and its cable railway on a wooden pier, T. H. Peacock's boat shop and storage yard, and a junk shop and blacksmith shop. Next to North 6th Street are The Cleveland Worsted Mills Co. and the Salisbury Worsted Mill, with the Camden Family Wash Laundry, and three rows of party-wall dwellings. Below Byron Street are two blocks of two-storey brick dwellings, with Troth's Camden Model Ware Ho. at the left. A compass rose stands in the park. Adjoining sheets are 38 below, 43 to the left and 45 on the right.
notes: Printed sheet number 44, previous edition sheets 22, 27 and 31 of volume 1.
Low confidence: three points form an exact fit.
North 5th Street is not on this sheet in the position OpenStreetMap suggests and was left out.
printed sheet 44, 50 ft: Pyne Point Park; three points, exact fit, low confidence

sheet-45.description: Sheet 45 is the northernmost sheet of Volume One, taking in a wide stretch of the Delaware River shore north of Erie Street. Most of the sheet is open river or open land with no buildings. Erie Street crosses the bottom edge, with North 8th Street and North 9th Street running north from it, each 60 ft wide, to the river. North 8th Street ends at a pointed inlet of the river, lettered as the Delaware River, and North 9th Street ends near a small square outline at the shore. Between them is a large undeveloped block numbered 2. West of North 8th Street a block numbered 1 contains the City Playground and the City Tennis Courts, drawn as rectangular plots with no buildings. The only building is a small one-storey office of the General Ship Repair Co. standing near the river on the left. A property line crosses the sheet near the top. A compass rose is drawn in the upper right. The left edge of the sheet is curved into the binding gutter, where part of a street name is cut off.
